Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Nobody is asked about their own phone. Say plainly that the person who breaks a trust is the one who did wrong. If a student is being targeted or something of theirs is being shared now, go with them to a counselor that day.

Every student in the room

Students whose private details get used against them (an eating disorder, being LGBTQ+, a disability, immigration status, money at home) carry the highest stakes; make clear that sharing someone else's secret is never fair just because it's true.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can explain why every message is a copy they don't control (screenshots, context collapse, online disinhibition), use the four-audience test before posting, and know what to do when something private gets shared, theirs or someone else's. The person who breaks a trust is the one who did wrong.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 3 minBefore we start
  2. 5 minHow far one screenshot spreads
  3. 7 minContext collapse and online disinhibition
  4. 3 minHow common it is
  5. 6 minThe four-reader check
  6. 5 minWhy people forward: turn and talk, share out
  7. 10 minThree situations: the class chat, Theo, Jordan
  8. 6 minIf it happens to you, every student, where else this shows up, close

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

How far one screenshot spreads, the four-reader check, one of the three situations, and if it happens to you.

Before you teach
Some students are living this now.

Someone in the room may have had a chat screenshotted or an image shared this year. Keep every example about the characters, and never use a real incident from your school.

Put the blame where it belongs.

Most people who get exposed trusted someone. Say it plainly: the person who breaks the trust did something wrong.

If a student is being threatened or harassed.

Thank them, help them document it (screenshots, account names, times), and walk them to a counselor that day. Threats over private images are urgent.

Be accurate about images.

In Massachusetts, sharing intimate images without consent is a crime, including AI fakes. Sexual images of anyone under 18 are illegal to create, keep or share even with agreement, and there's a diversion program for teen sexting. Say both halves.

Expect "but it was funny."

The party-video card usually brings this out. Ask how the person in the video would feel with everyone watching. That question does more than a lecture.

Keep the college piece in proportion.

Admissions officers say social media is fair game, but most don't check. Use it as one audience among four, not a scare tactic.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Private identities.

For an LGBTQ+ student who isn't out, or a student whose family's immigration status is private, one screenshot can carry real danger. When you talk about "someone else's secret," mention these without pointing at anyone.

Health and disability.

The group-chat card involves an eating disorder. Mental health, disability and medical details are among the most hurtful things to have spread. Treat the card seriously.

Family standards differ.

The four-audience test says "your family." Families differ on what's okay to share. Let students picture whoever raised them, or the relative whose opinion matters most.

Humor across cultures.

A joke built for five friends can read as racist or cruel to five hundred. Use the Harvard memes example to show how context collapse lands hardest on jokes about identity.

Language.

Messages in a home language can be translated and screenshotted too. Some students code-switch online; the same rules apply in every language.

Money and access.

Some students share one phone with siblings or a parent. Settings advice fits them too: tag approval and logging out matter even more on a shared device.

What the research says

Social media squeezes all your audiences into one (context collapse): friends, family, teachers and strangers.

Marwick and boyd, New Media and Society, 2011

People say things online they wouldn't face to face because there are no faces to read, no tone of voice, and a feeling that it doesn't count (online disinhibition).

Suler, CyberPsychology and Behavior, 2004

In 2022, 46% of 1,316 U.S. teens had experienced at least one form of cyberbullying; 22% had false rumors spread about them and 7% had explicit images shared without consent.

Vogels, Pew Research Center, 2022

Across 39 studies of more than 110,000 young people, about 12% had forwarded a sext without consent and about 8% had one of theirs forwarded.

Madigan et al., JAMA Pediatrics, 2018

67% of college admissions officers said applicants' social media is fair game, though only 28% said they had actually checked.

Kaplan survey, 2024

In 2017, Harvard rescinded admission offers to at least ten incoming students over offensive memes shared in a group chat they thought was private.

WBUR and Associated Press, 2017

Since 2024, sharing someone's intimate images without consent is a crime in Massachusetts, including AI fakes. The federal TAKE IT DOWN Act requires covered platforms to remove reported images within 48 hours.

Mass. Acts 2024, c. 118; TAKE IT DOWN Act, 2025
